reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A neurodevelopmental disorder with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and severely delayed or absent expressive speech
Neonatal hypotonia, autism spectrum disorder, and reduced perception of pain or altered sensory responses are characteristic
Minor dysmorphic features include a long face, full brow, dolichocephaly, large fleshy hands, and dysplastic toenails, but these can be subtle
Caused by deletion of the distal long arm of chromosome 22 (22q13.3) or by pathogenic SHANK3 variants, since loss of SHANK3 drives the core neurological phenotype
Most cases are de novo, but a proportion arise from an unbalanced translocation, so parental karyotype or array is important for recurrence-risk counselling
Regression, including loss of skills and psychiatric features such as bipolar-type illness or catatonia, can occur in adolescence or adulthood
Diagnosis relies on chromosomal microarray to size the deletion, with sequencing to detect intragenic SHANK3 variants when the array is normal
reference.pathophysiology: Phelan-McDermid syndrome results from loss of functional SHANK3 at chromosome 22q13.3, either through a terminal deletion of varying size or a pathogenic sequence variant. SHANK3 encodes a scaffolding protein at the postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses that organises glutamatergic signalling, so its haploinsufficiency impairs synapse formation and function, producing hypotonia, developmental delay, absent speech, and autistic features. Larger deletions remove additional genes, contributing to more extensive systemic and dysmorphic features and greater phenotypic severity.
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to detect and size the 22q13.3 deletion
SHANK3 sequencing when microarray is normal but the phenotype is suggestive
Parental chromosome/array studies to identify a balanced translocation and refine recurrence risk
Renal ultrasound and echocardiography for associated structural anomalies
Neurological review and, where regression occurs, psychiatric assessment
redFlags: Developmental or behavioural regression, or new catatonia or psychiatric illness in adolescence or adulthood
Absent pain perception masking serious injury or intra-abdominal pathology
Significant renal or cardiac anomaly identified on screening
reference.prognosis: Developmental disability and speech impairment are lifelong and most individuals need substantial support, while the risk of adolescent or adult regression and psychiatric illness adds long-term uncertainty. Larger deletions tend to correlate with greater severity, and multidisciplinary care improves quality of life.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as idiopathic autism without performing microarray and SHANK3 testing
Missing a parental balanced translocation and giving incorrect recurrence-risk advice
Overlooking reduced pain perception, which can delay recognition of injury or illness
Not anticipating and monitoring for regression and psychiatric change in later life
